headline: Fernley remains positive on global equities despite volatility, calling the AI investment cycle a once-in-a-lifetime capital spend with broad economic tailwinds

She stresses investors need to be more selective about what they own and must understand their AI exposures across all asset classes including infrastructure, private equity, and private credit. The key risk is not understanding the full extent of AI exposure within a portfolio rather than the AI theme itself failing.

Um, and that's an enormous tailwind. I think what we will see though is volatility. We're seeing it now. I think you need to be more careful what you own. And I think you need to make sure that you're across or across exactly what you do own in terms of AI. Um, because every single asset class is now impacted by it, whether that's infrastructure, whether that's the bond market, as we've just talked to, whether it's equities, private equity, private credit, it infiltrates your entire portfolio.

Massive capital spend is consistently surprising markets on the upside, making it very difficult to determine future returns on that capital. However, she believes the long-term productivity and innovation dividend will be real and broad-based across the economy. Volatility in individual names does not change the structural story.
quote: I think if we take a step back, the markets, um, not only stayed concentrated, but it's also got diverse at the same time. And that sounds a little strange, I know, but the key driver to everything remains AI. Um, it's an enormous capital spend, and the market is trying to determine what the return on invested capital will look like going forward. And what we know is that it is. If you look at any historical technological transformation, any of the historical and just think back to when the internet came through. Originally we thought that was all going to be, um, all about banner advertising, and it turned out to actually monetize very differently. And I suspect we suspect that the the AI story is still very much in the early innings. Um, but the the path to which we determine the economics, um, will be non-linear.

headline: US bond market facing indigestion as AI capex fundraising competes with $12 trillion Treasury refinancing, driving yields higher

Bid-to-cover ratios for hyperscaler IG paper have dropped from 4x to 1.5x, indicating market indigestion, while broader IG credit still attracts ~3x coverage. Equity issuance is also surging to ~$140 billion in 2026 versus $20–40 billion in recent years, adding further pressure across both markets and pushing yields higher.

There's just an enormous amount of debt demand. And what's really interesting is to actually see the bid to cover ratios that are coming through, um, in the market for hyper scalar CapEx what once had four times bid you know so oversubscription of four times. headline: Private credit systemic risk appears overhyped; bank results provide no corroborating evidence of widespread stress
reasoning: Fernley acknowledges there are pockets of real issues in private credit but argues the broader narrative is driven by hyperbole from commentators who don't fully understand the sector. Her key evidence is that bank charge-offs and delinquencies are not rising — if private credit stress were systemic, it would bleed through to bank results. She concludes there are always problem companies and governments, but the macro picture does not support a crisis thesis.
quote: And for everyone with this private credit story in their heads. If private credit was that problematic. You'd see it in the bank results as well. Yeah. And you're not. Do you think the private credit hype is high? I think there are pockets that it is real. But, you know, if it bleeds, it leads. Um, there's always this, um, hyperbole around the, the whole sector that I think is driven by, um, people talking about it that don't understand it. So there's no doubt there's some problem, but not really.

headline: Jacqueline Fernley argues AI investment cycle is early and multi-year, with further upside despite near-term volatility
reasoning: Fernley argues that AI-related capital expenditure is long-dated by definition, meaning the returns required are also long-dated and a single reporting season won't change the thesis. She notes the AI/tech segment continues to surprise positively and consistently relative to the broader market. She also observes that productivity benefits from AI have yet to flow through to the rest of the economy, suggesting further upside ahead. She acknowledges more volatility is likely but frames it as normal within a long bull cycle.
quote: I think the conclusion is that bubbles last a long time, a very long time, and we're early in two years and years of capital spend. Okay. There is capital by definition is long dated. So the returns attached to this capital that are required are also long dated. So one reporting season isn't going to change that. And the fact remains that the area in the market that is surprising more broadly and has been consistently remains the AI tech piece. And we're yet to even get the productivity benefits coming through the rest of the market. So I think we will get more volatility.

headline: AI investment winners are broadening out beyond the original Magnificent Seven, favouring equal-weight and small-cap exposure
reasoning: Fernley argues that AI is entering a new phase where the benefits are spreading across a wider set of companies, not just the concentrated mega-cap names that dominated last year. She cites companies like Intel, Alphabet, Tesla, and Texas Instruments as evidence of this broadening. The investment implication she draws is that expressing this through equal-weight ETFs or small-cap ETFs makes sense, as market performance is becoming less concentrated. She views this broadening as a positive development that does not undermine the longer-run productivity themes she has been discussing.
quote: I think Texas Instruments give me a really good sign of how AI is affecting these businesses. I think what you're seeing is you're seeing AI, um, broadening out, the winners starting to broaden out and the markets starting to go well. Last year we only needed to own these seven things. Now we can own a bit more. This is a good thing. So broadening out is a good thing. So for those for your viewers, the way you might express that is an equal weight ETF or a small cap ETF or moving towards some of those parts of the market, because we're not actually as concentrated in terms of performance as we were.

headline: Semiconductor supply chain volatility reflects normal demand-supply dynamics, not a structural AI bust; memory pricing surging on tight supply
reasoning: Fernley frames the chip sell-off as a routine supply chain lifecycle event driven by extraordinary demand rather than a negative inflection in AI investment. She highlights memory as an example where pricing and margins are surging because demand far outstrips supply. She acknowledges that Chinese chip competitors catching up to Nvidia is causing some multiple compression and profit-taking, and notes that investors in semiconductor ETFs who are up over 100% have natural incentive to take gains. She maintains the sector has still performed very well over the year.
quote: I think you're seeing just a normal life cycle through a supply chain, where you've got just an inordinate level of demand. Um, you've you're seeing an entire economy or global economy being driven by this enormous capital spend. Um, what does that mean? Well, someone that capital is being bought or bought, buying services or widgets. And then there's as a consequence of the supply chain around those widgets are, you know, some can respond to that demand. Some can't. And so prices go materially up. So what you're seeing with memory, for example, is margin and pricing going through the roof because demand is so high. So it's just movements around a supply chain which will balance out over time.
